nodes.description: The cornerstone of treatment. The standard regimen is an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (or streptomycin) for 2 months followed by isoniazid and rifampicin. The WHO regimen cited in the reviews totals 9 months; WHO guidance is also quoted as 6 to 9 months, while India's index guidelines recommend 12 months extendable to 18. The Medical Research Council trials found 6- and 9-month isoniazid-rifampicin regimens excellent and similar to 18-month regimens, a meta-analysis of six randomised studies found 6 months as effective as 9 months or more for healing (90.6% versus 87.3%), a pilot randomised trial of 100 biopsy-proven patients found 6 and 12 months equivalent, and a prospective study treating for 12 months found complete MRI healing in 30% at 6 months and 80% at 12 months. Duration is often individualised by clinical, laboratory and MRI response; patients not healing by 6 months should be investigated for drug resistance rather than simply treated for longer. Paradoxical worsening, a deterioration after the first month of treatment, occurred in 11% of a 73-patient series and predicted a poor outcome; it should not be mistaken for treatment failure. Drug-induced hepatitis occurred in 16% of the same series. Caveat: isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide are hepatotoxic, and treatment should be interrupted and a modified regimen used when ALT rises above three times the upper limit of normal with symptoms or jaundice, or five times without.

nodes.description: Collapse of one vertebra gives a knuckle, of two a gibbus and of more a rounded kyphosis. In children, kyphosis can progress during active disease and again after cure as the spine grows; radiological "spine at risk" instability signs predict a late increase, and the most severe form, buckling collapse beyond 120 degrees, is linked to infection before age seven, thoracolumbar disease and loss of more than two vertebral bodies.
